To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
The δ18O values of whole rock carbonaceous material from the Ordovician (Ordovician) are a function of temperature and the amount of ice on the Earth.

(a) the δ18O values of whole rock carbonaceous limestones are consistent with the interpretation that the ITCZ shifted southwards from its position at 10°S during the Hirnantian glaciation; (b) this southward shift was accompanied by a northward shift of the subtropical climate belt, and (c) the tropical climate belt was characterised by high SST and reduced SSS.

the δ18Ocarbs of the Ordovician faunas and carbonates from the tropical and subtropical regions are consistent with the results of the physical–chemical model and climate models, and suggest that the tropical water beneath the ITCZ was isotopically lighter than that of subtropical water.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the response of the tropical climate system to the onset of global glaciation during the Late Ordovician.
the evolution of the Inter-tropics Convergence Zone (ITCZ) and the response of the tropical climate to the onset of glaciation in Gondwana during the late Ordovician.

the response of the Inter-tropi-cal Convergence Zone to the onset of the Upper Ordovician glacial climate, as well as the impact of this glacial event on the distribution of faunal communities in low latitude regions.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the Ordovician climate was warm and humid and that the tropics were warmer than subtropical regions.
the ITCZ was shifted southward during the Hirnantian glaciation.
the ITCZ moved southward during the Hirnantian glaciation, and this is the first time such a statement can be made for the Ordovician.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the ITCZ was located in the equatorial region and that it shifted north and south in response to cooling in the southern hemisphere.
a global cooling of ~4°C and a salinity increase by ~1‰ occurred at the onset of the Late Ordovician ice age.
the tropical and subtropical water masses were warmer than today.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the Ordovician climate system was highly sensitive to changes in solar insolation.
the Ordovician tropical belt was not as narrow as previously thought, and that the tropical climate was much warmer than today.
the tropical and subtropical climate belts were not fixed but were displaced northwards during the Late Ordovician Glaciation (LOG) as the southern hemisphere cooled.
